concept.name: Calendar arbitrage
concept.definition: Trading the price relationship between futures (or options) on the same underlying with different expiration months - the intra-commodity calendar spread - by buying one expiry and selling another to capture changes in the term-structure gap rather than the outright price. Framed as arbitrage, it targets spreads that deviate from carry-implied or historical norms.
concept.intuition: March wheat and September wheat are the same wheat at different dates; the gap between them reflects storage, financing, and seasonal demand - trade the gap when it stretches beyond what carry justifies.
concept.mechanics: Buy the nearby (or deferred) month and sell the other as a single unit with two legs; P&L equals the change in the inter-month spread. Exchanges grant reduced margins on calendar spreads because systematic market risk largely nets out between the legs.
concept.formula: Spread P&L = (P_near,exit - P_near,entry) - (P_far,exit - P_far,entry); a spread narrowing from -11 to -8 cents on a 5,000-bushel wheat contract earns $150.
concept.failure_modes: Spreads are not bounded by delivery the way cash-futures convergence is: supply shocks, delivery squeezes in the nearby month, or storage-regime changes can run the spread far past fair carry, and liquidity in the deferred leg can be thin.
concept.misconceptions: That calendar spreads are slow and safe; nearby-month squeezes can move the spread more violently than the outright market, and the arbitrage framing is relative-value, not riskless.
concept.example: Buy March wheat at 526'6 and sell September at 537'6 (spread -11'0); when the spread narrows to -8'0, the 3-cent gain on the 5,000-bushel contract is $150 (Investopedia worked example).
